LEONARDO DA VINCI 346

whereby, through the weight it has gained, it increases in power and strikes with force against the water that previously overcame it, so that the line of the eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>circular or backward-flowing water patterns, such as whirlpools or eddies</note> bends in the opposite direction; where it was previously convex, it becomes concave. In this way, the smaller body of water is often pushed by the larger, and the larger is pushed by the smaller when the latter possesses less power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force, momentum, or kinetic energy of a current</note>.

->### CHAPTER XVI.<-

->*On the eddies formed by the impact of water against obstacles along the bank.*<-

Eddies are always generated between the columnar wave <term>onda colonnale</term> <note>a wave that rises in a column-like shape, often where currents meet or hit an obstacle</note> and the bank where such a wave has grown. This is proven because the water falls from the crest of the columnar wave toward the acceleration of the current, but it is pushed and pulled into the general flow of the water by the power of that current. The water likewise falls from the crest of the wave toward the bank (fig. 69, plate 13); but there, because the current is obstructed and delayed by the transverse motion of the same wave, it descends toward the bank, penetrating it with greater force, and by striking it <term>percotendola</term> <note>the act of the water hitting or "hammering" the bank</note>, creates an eddy.

->### CHAPTER XVII.<-

->*On the same.*<-

In every impact <term>percussione</term> <note>the forceful striking of water against a surface</note> of water against a narrowed bank or an obstacle in the bank, eddies are generated from the surface to the bottom. This is because, upon impact, the water rises up the height of the bank or obstacle, and gaining weight, it descends to the base. In the middle of this descent, it meets the water that had previously turned toward the bottom and is pushed back to the surface; there, overtaken by new arriving water and driven to the bottom in various swirls, it is carried along behind the main course of the water.

->### CHAPTER XVIII.<-

->*On the same.*<-

A bank that is set back to provide greater width to the canal will cause the immediate generation of an eddy. This is proven because the river, which acquires a sudden width, also acquires a sudden breadth of water, and the water that spreads out also decreases in depth;

<summary>Leonardo explains how eddies are formed by water striking obstacles or banks, describing a cycle where water rises upon impact, gains weight, and sinks to create vertical and horizontal rotations. He also notes that widening a channel creates immediate turbulence due to changes in water depth and breadth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s analysis of water behavior when striking a river bank. It specifically explores what happens when a narrow channel suddenly widens or encounters an obstacle, creating complex circular currents.</meta>

LEONARDO DA VINCI 347

therefore, a sudden current is generated, which, throwing itself against the widened bank <term>argine</term> <note>the side or levee of a river or canal</note>, strikes it and divides into two eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>circular or backward-flowing water patterns, such as whirlpools or eddies</note>.

## CHAPTER XIX.

->On the same.<-

Of the two eddies formed after the bank has widened, the first is the more powerful. Just as the eddy CBA (fig. 70. plate 13), by being enclosed, throws itself forcefully toward the bottom; and according to the forty-third [rule] of this treatise, which states that an eddy will have more penetrating force the less oblique the lip of its mouth is; this one will have it quite straight, etc. <note>Leonardo is referring back to a specific mathematical or physical proposition he established earlier in his notebook regarding the angle at which water enters a whirlpool.</note>

## CHAPTER XX.

->On the same.<-

If the channel should suddenly acquire width on every side, it generates eddies on every side, of which the first will be more powerful (fig. 71 plate 13). This is evident from the two previous chapters.

## CHAPTER XXI.

->On the same.<-

If the columnar wave <term>onda colonnale</term> <note>a wave that rises in a column-like shape, often where currents meet or hit an obstacle</note> strikes the eddies generated in one of the widened banks, then those enclosed eddies will become more constricted and will acquire great power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force, momentum, or kinetic energy of the water</note>. This happens not only because the columnar wave in such a case raises the water level, but also because by striking the bank itself, the force is multiplied, and the eddies remain more upright (fig. 72 plate 13).

## CHAPTER XXII.

->On the same.<-

If an object is placed in one of the widened banks beneath the columnar wave created by that object, the eddies that are generated will be of great power. This happens (fig. 73. plate 14) because where the water is most constricted by the object, the generated wave rises higher; for this reason, it descends toward the bank with greater impetus <term>impeto</term> <note>the momentum or surge of the water's movement</note>, and there eddies of greater power are created, etc.

<summary>Leonardo examines how sudden changes in a river's width or the presence of obstacles create powerful eddies, noting that the height of a wave directly increases the destructive force of the water against the bank.</summary>

## CHAPTER XXIII.
### *On the same subject.*

Wherever an obstacle is placed in a widened bank <term>argine</term> <note>the side, levee, or embankment of a watercourse</note> following its columnar waves <term>onde colonnale</term> <note>vertical surges or column-like waves formed by converging currents</note>, the eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>backward-flowing or circular currents, such as whirlpools or vortices</note> that strike the bank will be of greater power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force or kinetic energy of the water</note> than those that came before (fig. 74, plate 14). This is because the wave rises not only due to the narrowing of the channel, but also from the collision <unclear>of</unclear> one current with another; from this height, it descends toward the bank with greater impetus.

## CHAPTER XXIV.
### *On the same subject.*

If a side obstacle is placed that occupies a large part of the channel, not only will the aforementioned eddies strike its own bank, but eddies will also run from the surface to the bottom along the opposite bank. This happens because the water rises so high in the narrow mouth of the passage that, upon exiting, it does not only dash toward the bank—where the usual eddies are generated—but also falls to the bottom due to its own weight. There, in its rebound, it is oppressed by new falling water, and it revolves now below and now above, behind the path of the current.

## CHAPTER XXV.
### *On the same subject.*

If two equal side obstacles are placed, not only are lateral revolutions created at the banks after the water's discharge, but various circulations from the surface to the bottom also go revolving in the middle; this is manifest from the seventeenth [rule] and the previous one.

## CHAPTER XXVI.
### *On the eddies created by the impact of water against obstacles on the bottom underwater.*

If a rock <term>scoglio</term> <note>a submerged rock, reef, or large stone obstacle</note> that divides the flow of the water only in its lower parts is covered by the flowing water, the water passing over the top will fall behind it, landing at its base. The water that falls from such a depth swirls in a backward-spinning motion <note>original: "revertiginosamente"; Leonardo describes a complex, turbulent spiral that turns back against the main flow.</note> both below and above, because...

<summary>Leonardo explains how obstacles in a river channel—whether on the banks or submerged—create powerful eddies and vertical circulations that can erode the riverbed and embankments.</summary>

Wang Rong, while in prison, composed a response to an interrogation stating: The respect shown to those of high and low rank is different. Zhu Zhicai's poem for the Seventh Night of the Seventh Month <note>the Qixi Festival</note> says: The Gourd and the Ox <note>constellations</note> carry the trays, how can the golden shuttle be thrown to the ground? It is utterly absurd.

### High Rank
History of Yuan, Annals of Emperor Yingzong: In the various districts and counties of the vast coastal regions, there are many vacant official posts. Those who are honest and willing to take these positions shall be advanced two grades in rank.

### Private Rank
Han Feizi: When Jisun was the minister of Lu, Zilu served as the magistrate of Hou. The state of Lu mobilized the masses in the fifth month to dig a long trench. During this task, Zilu used his own grain to make congee and rice to feed the laborers at the crossroads of Wufu.

### Combined Rank
Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals: The method of examination is to match one's title and salary <note>original: "jue lu"</note> with their combined rank, calculate their days of service, and display their merits.

### Full Rank
Garden of Stories <note>original: "Shuo Yuan"</note>: Uncle Fan of Jin said: If the people have the appearance of hunger while the horses have the appearance of fullness, the ruler cannot maintain his position. Yan Yanzhi's Rhapsody on the Red and White Horse: They are placed in the depths of the Washing Dragon Pond and entrusted with the fodder of the Red Grain Storehouse.

### Supply Rank
Garden of Stories: Yanzi said: Now we speak of seeking out the elderly and weak who are not cared for, and the widowed and orphaned who are not recognized; these are discussed as having a lowly rank.

### Many Ranks
Discourses Weighed in the Balance <note>original: "Lunheng"</note>: King Cheng's talent was not equal to the Duke of Zhou; Duke Huan's wisdom was not equal to Guan Zhong. Yet Cheng and Huan received the mandate of honor, while Zhou and Guan received the mandate of rank. Zhang Jiuling's poem: In my later years, following many ranks, the fork in the road is truly not singular. Ouyang Xiu's poem: Diligent yet ashamed of clever officialdom, in poverty and lowliness I keep my many ranks.

### Gracious Rank
Xie Lingyun's poem: Having completed my term, how could I expect a gracious rank? Xie Zhuang's Memorial on Seeking Talent: Some are advanced in rank on the spot, others enter into the glory and favor of the court.

### Concurrent Rank
Xie Tiao's poem: Hurriedly going to serve at the Southern Peak, concurrently holding a rank with the name of the state.

### Retired Rank
Xie Tiao's poem: Resigning due to illness without waiting for the usual age, keeping one's retired rank. Emperor Yuan of Liang's Decree on Encouraging Farming: At the time when the Star Bird <note>a constellation marking spring</note> appears, it signals the year's prosperity in the spring; the Resting Dragon song is heard as the harvest is taken from the southern fields.

### Refined Rank
Jiang Hai's Petition on Taking the Proper Position: The path of the woodcutter follows the flourishing industry; great blessings and abundant prosperity are attained through refined rank.

## INTRODUCTION.

---

The "Sepher Yetzirah," <note>original: "Sepher Yetzirah," meaning "Book of Formation"</note> or "Book of Formation," is perhaps the oldest philosophical treatise still in existence written in the Hebrew language. The great interest shown in recent years regarding the Hebrew Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a traditional system of Jewish mysticism and self-knowledge</note> and its related schools of thought has led me to translate this volume from the original Hebrew texts, comparing them with the Latin versions produced by medieval scholars. Three important books of the "Zohar," or "Splendor"—which serves as the primary storehouse of Kabbalistic teaching—have been translated into English for the first time by the skillful and learned Kabbalist MacGregor Mathers, my fellow student in the occult sciences. If, however, on the day of the first summons of the warrantors, both the petitioner and the tenant do not stand because of that, let him take by default if the jurors were present; if not, then there will be another day, and the warrantors, when they have offered themselves until the fourth day, and then concerning the record of himself concerning the warranty, it will not be able to be used to the day on which it remained before, etc. Because not received immediately here, another remains in force by default [in such a way] that there may not be [anyone] who may be attached there, he may be [prayed], it is able to be that which if he has not come and if any were by his great [default], and he estimates and would go out, all then he would ask concerning the whole, then from above let him fear to him. If, however, the petitioner does not pray, the fourth day having been awaited, let the tenant recede from those, and similarly the warrantors. If, however, the petitioner were [present] and the warrantor has made default, then before all things for the default of the warrantor, let him first take the assize by default into the use of the warrantor, and at the day of the witnesses by proper land as in another manner, unless before he [had] his assent whether the tenant has lost or remits it, and then it will be then let the warrantor proceed in himself the warrantor, and where if on the first day the assize cannot be taken but [it remains].

<margin>Warantus inveniri non potest in villa nec in patria</margin> Casus iste incidit in itinere in Norfolcia haeres Anno regis Henrici filii regis Iohannis decimo nono ad medium quadragesimae. Si autem huiusmodi terra vacua de ambo monasterio remanet et vocatur ad warrantum Willelmus de Albo Monasterio et quod de terra talis videtur. Warantus cum venit non vocat ad warrantum sed dicit pro se de terra videlicet vel duos ex plebibus warantum capienda est assisa si viderit plene: rescripta fecit. Et primum si per manum iustitiarii qui assisam capiat per rescriptum ad eundem die capti assisa si differat captio usque ad alium diem et warantus tunc venit per districtionem vel sive et ad warrantizandum noluerit aut capione assisae ubi poterit non tunc ad defensionem ut res remanet defendatur vel ad dicendum si assisam ubi debeat fieri aut si tenens amittat per assisam in nullo fovetur per captionem assisae quia non est ante quasi in possessionem quin possit defendere tenens nisi ad excambium propter warantiam et si vultus pro ipso warantizant quo ad excambium videtur warantus vocare in periculum pro re si ipse sit vel per alium qualis ipse sit in iustitia. Et si unus sit unus feoffator et qui warantus suus possit esse de cetero in seisina et quod assisa capi debeat per defectum waranti statim per defectum habet certum diem scilicet anno regis Henrici filii regis Iohannis decimo nono cum fuit assisa ad medium quadragesimae filia de tenemento in villa unde videlicet ubi rex de terra illa tenuit. Vocavit inde ad warrantum Petrum de sed laudo de Rotomago qui pulsatus fuit de ultra mare rex de facto fecit. Et non obstante sicut quia assisa procedat ipsa cessante ipsi poterit. Et quia ubi amittit per assisam hinc rex fuit in possessione. Et videtur etiam quod non erit ad capiendum in tenemento ad valentiam de terra secundum quod warantus vocatus sit in warantum neque suum ad capiendam assisam de eis secundum curiam anno Henrici regis decimo octavo cum Bukerel ad medium quadragesimae. <margin>Si warantus tenens de facto fecerit</margin> Et sciendum est quod si tenens cum warantizatum sit per se vel alium non vult respondere de warantia cum non sit dominus et sequatur ubi aliquis de terra et warantus ad primum diem venit et se defendit de warantia non erit ad assisam tenens et warantus diebus poterit de aliis diebus remanente debeat tenens non propter defensionem suam solvit in warantiam quod de tenemento non per warantum aut cum non tenuerit diebus et alium in defende et defendit se de warantia non tenet hoc per praefatam virtutem capiat assisa. <margin>Si warantus de facto non sit</margin> Si autem warantus de facto non sit si primo die optulit se ad respondendum si petens tunc petere tenet aut statim warantizat aut opponit contra quem warantizare non debeat et si statim warantizat tunc inde procedat assisa tunc remanet relaxat ipse tunc vel ad respondendum cum omni bene caveat a defensione et per hoc patet hic tenetur infra videtur et forte placet eis si qui tenens autem teneat de feodo iustitiarii et sic per se defendit statum in ipsa warantia unum vel plures qui ad defensionem per panem vel notam pro warantia aut warantizant alii et sic invicem successive et si summo celeriter per auxilium vel sine et qui ultimo sequi debeat Simonem ille de warantia teneatur ibidem suum rotulorum per experimentum iustitiarii ad rectum quod habet pervenire de tenemento cum warantizant nihil la fiat mentio. Et tenens remanebit tenens sicut plurimi petere et warantus qui favet defensionem et si petens vocaverit tenentem de waranto in warantum et ultimus de se cesset capio. <margin>Hoc cum plures sunt waranti et ultimus tenere non possit</margin> Et cum plures sunt waranti et ultimus tenere non possit in assisa per defectum waranti capiat et ultimus warantus de excambio faciendo se defendendo non possit facere excambium suo feoffato et id excambium revertetur ad primum tenentem de manu in manum de waranto in warantum in quantum plene dicet de warantia. Si autem videlicet ex plebibus in patria vel plures sint infra aetatem ubi illorum et aetate expectet breve. Si autem unus ex plebibus petentibus igitur ante captionem assisae

<column-break/>

moriatur non tunc propter hoc cadit breve sed remanebit assisa ut de itinere Willelmi de Ralegh in comitatu Warwicensi anno regis Henrici decimo octavo in fine itineris ad obsequium domini regis in vice sua ubi monachus expulit tenentem de terra et ubi si assisa omnino sit de hoc naturaliter enim me plene praecepit quod fuit huiusmodi si ubi monachus eadio alla et ibi de hoc sicut rex pro se non tenet de feoffamento vel si ut monachus non tunc propter hoc cadit breve et sic si ipse tenens vel tenens ubi ubi monachus et eadem loquela omnino si de faciente substantiam. Si autem warantus ut praeceptum est per breve remaneat et tunc iustitiarii warantizavit vel non. Si autem non warantizavit non cadit per mortem waranti sed incipiat tenens vocare suum heredem de novo. Si autem warantizavit sicut secundum quod aliquis warantizavit sit quasi principalis et si tenens pro fuerit in warantiam defensione sua omnino in illa resumit breve quod non est in praesentia tunc quod movetur quod ad plenam autem breve iam ubi ostentat si autem warantus videlicet vel unus ex plebibus cui plene successive vocentur se defendere de warantia quod warantus non debeat ulla alia sibi poena si quod capiat assisa per defectum et si per tenentem observatur id ipsum per excambium cum ei fuerit semel warantizatum et assisa capi debeat statim per defectum secundum iustitiarium de re per ipsum Simonem Anno regis Henrici decimo octavo ad medium quadragesimae apud Westmonasterium de terra de michem de ralinge in comitatu Simoni de okeray. <margin>Bukerel</margin> Et ad medium quadragesimae si warantus warantizare non debeat quod ulla sibi poena nisi quod assisa capietur et tunc quod warantus se assisa defendere debeat si amittit per assisam tunc debeat remanere si tunc die scilicet propter assisam rassa aufert vel dat iustitiarii postquam iustitiarii non possunt videret et defendere ipsum nisi die petens nihil habeat de hoc et si facere non possit unde capiat ubi alia # DE IVREIVRANDO <gloss>ON THE TAKING OF OATHS</gloss>

### THESIS I.

<meta>Large ornamental initial C</meta>Since the religious <term>iusiurandum</term> <gloss>oath</gloss> has come into use as the greatest remedy for settling disputes—by which controversies are decided either through the agreement of the litigants themselves or by the authority of a judge—the <term>Praetor</term> <gloss>magistrate</gloss> has not undeservedly announced that he will compel the person from whom an oath is requested to either satisfy the request or take the oath.

### II.

However, another faculty is granted to the defendant, namely that if he prefers, he may refer the oath <note>to the plaintiff</note>, although it is not always consonant in every way for the oath to be referred in the same manner it was offered.

### III.

But we understand this only regarding a judicial oath.

### IIII.

For an oath is either voluntary, judicial, or necessary.

### V.

We call it voluntary when it is offered by one litigant to another by agreement outside of court.

### VI.

We call it judicial when it is offered by a litigant to a litigant within the court.

### VII.

It is necessary when a judge offers it to one of the litigants in doubtful cases or in the absence of proofs.

### VIII.

Likewise, this necessity of taking an oath ceases if the one who offered the oath, upon the demand of the adversary, refuses to swear regarding <term>calumnia</term> <gloss>malicious intent/bad faith in litigation</gloss>, and it is held as if the oath had been remitted.

<summary>Introduction to the types of oaths in legal disputes, specifically distinguishing between voluntary, judicial, and necessary oaths.</summary>

This oath regarding <term>calumnia</term> <gloss>malicious intent</gloss> is nevertheless remitted for the advocate and for parents. Nor is it offered to the one who refers it.

X.
For which reasons also a person is not compelled to accept a judgment, nor is he to be compelled to swear that he is not obligated to give <note>or pay</note> something.

XI.
By a constitution of <term>Justinian</term> <gloss>Roman Emperor and legal reformer</gloss>, it was also effected that an oath not yet performed, having been revoked by the one who offered it, cannot be offered to the adversary again.

XII.
Finally, an oath is not to be accepted, nor is an accepted one valid, except when offered by those who are competent to do so.

XIII.
Therefore, an oath offered by a ward, a person under twenty-five years of age, a spendthrift, or a madman will be held as not offered. The same law applies to a slave and a son-in-power, unless they have the administration of their <term>peculium</term> <gloss>private fund/assets</gloss>.

XIIII.
The tutor of a ward, however, when all other proofs are lacking, rightly offers the oath.

XV.
The act of a <term>procurator</term> <gloss>legal representative/proxy</gloss> who offers an oath is to be held as ratified: namely, if he sustains the administration of all goods, or if the thing itself is specifically mandated, or if the procurator acts in his own interest.

XVI.
Otherwise, however, it was responded by <term>Julian</term> <gloss>famous Roman jurist</gloss> that a procurator offering an oath is not to be heard.

In this, the author rebukes the master for vices. The first is lying, in that he who does this commits a lie, which must be shunned. Master <term>Aeneas</term> <note>Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini</note> in his letters: Nothing is more consistent than truth; nothing is more inconsistent and unstable than a lie. Second, he rebukes vainglory; since it is empty and transitory, a continent person ought to flee it. Third duty: that poverty itself ought not to be unclean to you, because God loves it. Master <term>Juvenal</term> in his satire: Happy are the poor people whom the spirit will love. It now draws them back to the sublime kingdom. Fourth duty: that the parsimony of the continent person ought not to be sordid, this is, the abstinence of the continent ought not to be foul. Because abstinence is a virtue. Master, the name of parsimony or abstinence can be taken in two ways according to blessed <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the <term>Secunda Secundae</term>, question 146, article 1. One way, as it denotes the absolute subtraction of food. And in this way it does not signify an act of virtue, but is something indifferent. Another way, according to how it is regulated by reason, and in that way it designates a habit or an act of virtue. And he defines it thus: It is the moderate taking or subtraction of food according to reason. And that ought not to be sordid, just as is some abstinence of hypocrites and misers, etc. Fifth duty is that the continent person's simplicity ought not to be neglected; this is, the humility of the continent ought not to be slow. Master, that simplicity itself is said to be neglected when it does not perform good works, namely, when someone acts otherwise than his intention, so that with his simplicity he may deceive others. Master <term>Alanus</term> <gloss>Alanus de Insulis</gloss> in his proverbs: Do not hold everything to be gold that shines, like gold; nor every beautiful apple to be good. Virtue is in many things where it is not seen; our lights deceive with their deeds, etc. Sixth, that the levity of the continent person ought not to be languid; this is, the mobility of the soul ought not to be infirm or weak. Master, then levity is said to be infirm or languid when the soul of man is moved more to the lower things, this is, to the operation of temporal things, than to those things which are above. Seventh, that the continent person ought not to be anguished, moreover, because his possessions are small to him. Master <term>Lato</term> <note>likely referring to a philosophical tradition or specific aphorism</note>: Nature created you an infant, naked; remember to bear the burden of poverty patiently. Because poverty having mixed joy is safe and secure. Eighth, that the continent person ought not to weep for his lost goods, because they are a gift of fortune. Master <term>Seneca</term> in a certain letter to <term>Lucillus</term>: There is nothing that fortune has made yours. As if he were saying: the gifts of fortune are variable and doubtful. Therefore, a temperate person ought not to be sad about the loss of temporal things. Ninth, that the continent person ought not to highly praise another’s goods, as is the custom of men. Master <term>Virgil</term>: The crop is always more fertile in another's field, and the neighbor’s cattle have a larger udder.

> Do you punish another more than you are yourself
> And love truth at all times
> And avoid lies always, most steadily

In this part, <term>Seneca</term> sets forth five duties of <term>temperantia</term> <gloss>temperance</gloss> with regard to another species, which is called modesty. The first duty: that you, a continent person, ought to flee base things before they happen; this is, not only in effect but also in the affect of the vices, to restrain yourself. The second duty: You, a continent person, ought not to rebuke anyone more than yourself. This is, you ought to correct yourself first. And then strike another. <term>Cato</term> says: Do not do the things yourself that you are accustomed to blame. It is shameful for a teacher when his own guilt refutes him. Rebuking is twofold, namely, of the soul and of the body. Of the soul is that which is held on the part of the soul, and the master speaks of that here. The other is of the body, which is held on the part of the body, and such is again to be shunned. The third duty: that you, a continent person, can endure all things that are to be sustained, except baseness. For the <term>temperantia</term> of the virtue of <term>temperantia</term>, a virtuous person is called; therefore, he ought to avoid those things which are opposite to virtue. And baseness is a vice in itself, therefore it is to be shunned. The fourth duty: you, a continent person, ought to abstain from base words, which immodesty nourishes. For earlier in the <term>Ethics</term>, each one operates according to what he is. If therefore he is good and virtuous, he works good things; if therefore he is base, he works base things. The fifth duty: you, a continent person, ought to love utility in your sermons more than ornament. The reason: that useful words edify the intellect. If they are eloquent, they impede the inquiry of truth. According to that of the philosopher in the first <term>Perihermenias</term> <gloss>On Interpretation</gloss>, poetic and oratorical speeches are to be declined, that is, dismissed, because they rather impede the inquiry of truth than clarify it. Therefore, <term>Vincentius</term> in the <term>Speculum Historiale</term> <gloss>Historical Mirror</gloss>, book seven, says it is base and very vicious to bring forward delicate sentences which are not understood by many. Furthermore, you, a continent person, ought to love fruitful sermons more than eloquent ones.

<summary>Seneca discusses modesty and temperance, emphasizing self-correction, the avoidance of baseness, and the preference for useful, honest speech over merely eloquent or flowery language.</summary>
